_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: UT Dallas researchers paired satellite air readings with CDC cancer data for every Texas county. Dirtier counties tended to have more cancer, and the authors say what that can't prove.

introduction.text: [A team in UT Dallas's School of Economic, Political and Policy Sciences studied all {{number:c1}} Texas counties and found geographic associations between air pollution and cancer prevalence](c1). [It used public CDC data on cancer prevalence and satellite data on air pollution](c2), [and applied a machine learning method to the correlations](c3).

[The satellites measured eight air pollutants in {{number:c4}}, among them sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, formaldehyde and methane](c4). [The readings came from the Sentinel-5 Precursor satellite and the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service](c23). [The paper went online {{date:c11}} in Environmental Monitoring and Assessment](c11).

paragraphs.text: [Counties with more pollution tended to have more cancer](c5). [Sulfur dioxide was the most influential environmental predictor](c6). [The paper compared four machine learning algorithms](c20), [and a support vector machine fit the data best](c21). [Rahman says socioeconomic and other variables were controlled for](c27).

[Fangchao Dong, a doctoral student and co-corresponding author, describes three major clusters of air pollution in Texas](c7). [The east part of the state is worse in air quality, the west is better and the central part sits in between](c8). [Counties with higher cancer prevalence tended to sit near others with similarly high prevalence rather than at random](c9).

[Collecting pollution data from monitors on the ground is costly, which has limited this kind of spatial analysis](c13). [Remote sensing let the team look at air pollution across all of Texas](c17), [and the paper says satellite data can support health assessment where ground monitoring is unavailable](c25). [Rahman says the method can also show where medical centers are and where government should focus](c14).

[The study did not find that every more polluted place had more cancer](c10), [and the researchers say cancer reflects many influences besides pollution](c19). [They say the results are not sufficient evidence of a causal link between pollution and cancer risk in any one person](c11).

[Satellite readings may also be less precise than readings from ground monitors](c12), [and the team wants more research on the cost and accuracy of the approach](c18). The published findings describe places, so a reader can't use them to judge the risk to a particular person or to rank a particular county.
